Reproductive ecology in the Western shovelnose stingaree (Trygonoptera mucosa) is characterised by relatively slow life-history traits typical of many urolophid rays. At a stable water temperature of 22 °C [T = 22 °C], the gestation period extends to approximately 335.5 days [ab = approximately 335.5 days], a duration comparable to that reported for other viviparous batoids in temperate Australian waters. Newborn individuals emerge from the female at a modest disc width of 12 cm [Lb = 12 cm], placing them among the smaller neonates within the family Urolophidae. This size at birth reflects an extended reliance on yolk reserves during development, with the yolk sac providing the sole nutritional source throughout the embryonated phase. Females invest considerable energy in each pup, which likely contributes to the relatively low fecundity observed in this species. The reproductive cycle appears to be biennial or triennial in many populations, a pattern that aligns with the slow somatic growth and late maturity documented for stingarees inhabiting temperate continental shelf environments across southern Australia.

Juveniles undergo a prolonged period of somatic growth before the onset of gonadal differentiation and eventual sexual maturation. The disc width at which females first exhibit signs of pubertal development has been estimated at 25 cm [Lp = 25 cm], a threshold that represents approximately 68 percent of their ultimate adult disc width. In contrast, males reach puberty at a noticeably smaller body size of 22 cm [Lp = 22 cm] in disc width, indicating a pronounced sexual dimorphism in the timing of reproductive system activation. This divergence is consistent with patterns observed across multiple elasmobranch taxa, where males typically mature at a smaller proportion of their asymptotic size. Data obtained from field surveys and captive holding studies suggest that the transition from a reproductively immature juvenile to a pubertal individual is correlated with accumulation of sufficient lipid reserves. The specific somatic growth rate during this period appears sensitive to local prey availability and bottom-water temperature regimes commonly encountered on the continental shelf.

The maximum disc width attained by adult females is 36.9 cm [Li = 36.9 cm], representing the asymptotic body size beyond which further skeletal growth is negligible. Males reach a considerably smaller ultimate disc width of 28.3 cm [Li = 28.3 cm], reinforcing the pronounced sexual size dimorphism evident in this species. The corresponding ultimate wet weight for females, derived from a length-weight relationship based on the congener Trygonoptera testacea, is approximately 2200 grams [Wwi = approximately 2200 grams], reflecting the substantial investment in body mass required for a viviparous reproductive mode. Males achieve a much lower maximum weight of roughly 1010 grams [Wwi = roughly 1010 grams], a difference that aligns with the energetic demands of gestation and parturition in females. Field capture records indicate that individuals approaching these asymptotic dimensions are uncommon, suggesting that few rays survive to reach full somatic potential under natural conditions, likely due to predation pressure and fisheries interactions across their range.

Age-based demographic parameters have been investigated primarily through captive observations and vertebral banding analyses conducted at a controlled temperature of 22 °C [T = 22 °C]. Under these thermal conditions, female Western shovelnose stingarees exhibit a maximum lifespan of approximately 5840 days [am = approximately 5840 days], which corresponds to roughly 16 years, while males have a shorter maximum longevity of around 10 years [am = around 10 years] at a temperature of 22 °C [T = 22 °C]. This sex-based disparity in lifespan, with females outliving males by roughly six years, aligns with the general pattern observed in many elasmobranchs wherein the larger sex tends to exhibit greater survivorship. These longevity estimates place Trygonoptera mucosa among the shorter-lived members of the Urolophidae, though direct comparisons are limited by a scarcity of demographic data for related species. The age-specific mortality schedule remains poorly characterised, but adult survival appears to be relatively high given the prolonged reproductive tenure required to offset low annual fecundity.

Reproductive output is limited, with females producing a single pup per reproductive event [N_R_i = single pup per reproductive event] and, at 22 °C [T = 22 °C], achieving a maximum of approximately 1.1 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 1.1 litters per year]. This low fecundity is typical of batoid species that invest heavily in individual offspring size and maternal provisioning. The maximum reproduction rate, expressed as pups per female per year at the optimum temperature, is thus approximately 1.1 pups annually, a figure that underscores the species' vulnerability to population depletion. Given the prolonged gestation, late age at maturation, and minimal annual reproductive output, population growth potential is severely constrained, making Trygonoptera mucosa particularly susceptible to mortality from trawl bycatch, which is the primary anthropogenic threat across much of its distribution in southern Australian waters. Conservation assessments for this data-deficient species would benefit from more detailed demographic modelling and improved fisheries reporting.
